newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Hanoi sounds alarm on state sector capital crunch.
newsitem.headline: Hanoi sounds alarm on state sector capital crunch.

text.p: Vietnam's lumbering state sector needs hundreds of millions of dollars in fresh funding to get back on an even keel, according to a Ministry of Finance report.

Vietnam Economic Times said on Friday that the report put state-owned enterprises' capital needs at 10 trillion dong ($857 million), of which 30 percent would have to be found over the next 12 months.

The official weekly also carried an interview with Finance Minister Nguyen Sinh Hung, who said new funding for state-owned enterprises' (SOEs) working capital would come from the central government budget, the central bank and retained profits.
Hung described the injection of capital as "one step back to take two forward".
Concern has been mounting in recent months over the failing health of SOEs, especially with signs that the economy is starting to slow after several years of stellar growth.

A recent report by Swedish economists warned that the benefits of the communist country's decade-old reform drive may be close to exhaustion without reforms in trade and a rethink of policies which favour state enterprises.

"...it is not much of an exaggeration to characterise the present financial situation of the SOE sector as a time bomb," it said, adding that in 1995 the sector's aggregate debt amounted to around $24 billion, some 20 percent more than aggregate turnover.
The number of state-owned firms has been halved to around 6,250 as part of the reforms in an effort to cut away dead wood.

However, the vast majority still run at a loss and a recent government survey found that the sector is among the most inefficient in the world, using equipment that belongs in museums and suffering from an almost total lack of automation.
Hung said that borrowing procedures for SOEs would be simplified and a regulation limiting their loans to no more than 10 percent of their fixed assets would be scrapped.
The government will also write off some of the SOEs' overdue debt to state-owned banks as part of the injection of capital.
Hung added that capital support would be biased towards SOEs which produce food products for export or those involved in infrastructure projects.
